extracted.intended_audience: poets, students, and readers interested in poetic forms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing, composing, and distinguishing types of sonnets (their lineation, rhyme schemes, structural divisions, and notable variations). Useful for poets, students, and teachers learning formal properties of sonnets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional sonnet definition (line count and typical purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 14-line poem with a variable rhyme scheme originating in Italy and brought to England ... Literally a “little song,” the sonnet traditionally reflects upon a single sentiment, with a clarification or “turn” of thought in its concluding lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core identifying features: 14 lines (though there are notable variations), focus on a single sentiment or idea, and an expected concluding 'turn' (volta) that clarifies or shifts the poem's thought. Use this as the baseline when labeling or composing a sonnet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volta (turn of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sonnet traditionally reflects upon a single sentiment, with a clarification or “turn” of thought in its concluding lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating a sonnet, look for a structural or tonal shift (often near the octave/sestet break in Petrarchan forms or before/within the final couplet in English/Shakespearean forms) that reframes or resolves the preceding material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petrarchan sonnet (structure and rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petrarchan sonnet divides the 14 lines into two sections: an eight-line stanza (octave) rhyming ABBAABBA, and a six-line stanza (sestet) rhyming CDCDCD or CDECDE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate octave/sestet division and the prescribed rhyme patterns. Examples given: Milton’s “When I Consider How my Light Is Spent” and Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s “How Do I Love Thee.” The volta typically occurs between the octave and sestet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian sonnet (English variation of the Petrarchan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Italian sonnet is an English variation on the traditional Petrarchan version. The octave’s rhyme scheme is preserved, but the sestet rhymes CDDCEE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying this variation, confirm the ABBAABBA octave and the CDDCEE sestet. Examples: Thomas Wyatt’s “Whoso List to Hunt, I Know Where Is an Hind” and John Donne’s “If Poisonous Minerals, and If That Tree.”

rubrics_metrics.name: English (Shakespearean) sonnet (quatrains + couplet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wyatt and Surrey developed the English (or Shakespearean) sonnet, which condenses the 14 lines into one stanza of three quatrains and a concluding couplet, with a rhyme scheme of ABABCDCDEFEFGG (though poets have frequently varied this scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess three quatrains that develop aspects of an argument or situation and a final couplet that often provides a resolution, epigrammatic turn, or summary. Note that many poets adapt or vary the rhyme scheme; examples include George Herbert’s “Love (II),” Claude McKay’s “America,” and Molly Peacock’s “Altruism.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Spenserian sonnet (interlocking rhyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spenserian sonnet is a 14-line poem ... that varies the English form by interlocking the three quatrains (ABAB BCBC CDCD EE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the linking rhyme pattern across quatrains (each quatrain borrows a rhyme from the preceding one) and the final couplet EE. Origin: Edmund Spenser’s Amoretti.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caudate sonnet (adds coda or tail)
rubrics_metrics.description: The caudate sonnet, which adds codas or tails to the 14-line poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A standard 14-line sonnet base is present but is extended by one or more additional lines ('tail' or coda). Example: Gerard Manley Hopkins’s “That Nature Is a Heraclitean Fire.” Use this when a sonnet-like argument continues beyond the fourteenth line as an intentional formal device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curtal sonnet (Hopkins's shortened variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: A curtailed sonnet: a shortened version devised by Gerard Manley Hopkins that maintains the proportions of the Italian form, substituting two six-stress tercets for two quatrains in the octave (rhyming ABC ABC), and four and a half lines for the sestet (rhyming DEBDE), also six-stress except for the final three-stress line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter and proportional relationships matter here: the curtal preserves the proportional feel of an Italian sonnet in a compressed line-count. Example: Hopkins’s “Pied Beauty.” When evaluating, note both rhyme pattern and the stressed-syllable counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet redoublé / crown of sonnets (linked-sonnet form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sonnet redoublé, also known as a crown of sonnets, is composed of 15 sonnets that are linked by the repetition of the final line of one sonnet as the initial line of the next; the last sonnet consists of all the repeated lines of the previous 14 sonnets, in the same order in which they appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a multi-sonnet structural constraint: to evaluate or compose one, verify the linking/repetition of lines across the sequence and that the final sonnet assembles the repeated lines. Contemporary example: Marilyn Nelson’s A Wreath for Emmett Till.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet sequence (grouping and thematic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sonnet sequence is a group of sonnets sharing the same subject matter and sometimes a dramatic situation and persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a sequence, look for thematic continuity, recurring persona, or a developing dramatic situation across multiple sonnets. Examples: George Meredith’s Modern Love, Sir Philip Sidney’s Astrophel and Stella, Rupert Brooke’s 1914 sequence, Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s Sonnets from the Portuguese.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stretched sonnet (extended line-count)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stretched sonnet is extended to 16 or more lines, such as those in George Meredith’s sequence Modern Love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the poet intentionally exceeds the 14-line norm to expand argument or narrative; treat the extended length as a formal choice rather than a misapplied label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submerged sonnet (sonnet within a longer work)
rubrics_metrics.description: A submerged sonnet is tucked into a longer poetic work; see lines 235-48 of T.S. Eliot’s “The Waste Land.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a discrete 14-line (or sonnet-proportioned) section embedded within a longer poem; consider how the sonnet's turn and compact argument function inside the larger work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme-scheme variability and poetical adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many different types of sonnets. ... (noting) poets have frequently varied [schemes].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing sonnets, allow for historical and creative variation: poets may adapt rhyme schemes, stanza divisions, or lineation to suit voice and intention. Use the canonical schemes as guides rather than absolute rules.
